title: Prepare a welcoming space without sacrificing household needs

sections.title: Understand the distinction
sections.body: Hospitality creates a welcome within household capacity and boundaries. It does not require money, private-room access or removing another resident’s supports.

sections.title: Complete fictional practice material
sections.body: Fictional visit: Rae is welcome Saturday 14:00–14:30, prefers a chair and quiet conversation, and needs the existing clear entrance route. Resident Jo shares the room with Kim, whose reachable work materials must remain in place. Two chairs and tap water are available; no food is promised. Kim agrees to a 30-minute visit and no background music. No medical explanation is requested.

sections.title: Work through the supplied case
sections.body: Plan the route, seat, simple welcome and ending. Identify one arrangement that would burden the household rather than improve the visit.

sections.title: Try a different case before checking
sections.body: A host offers a luxurious meal by spending money needed for an essential household bill. Does generosity alone make the arrangement sound?

checks.title: Compare reasoning and review the supplied result
checks.body: Use the available chair and clear route, offer water without pressure, keep Kim’s materials and end at 14:30. Later fiction: Rae leaves 14:20 and says the quiet helped; no broader inclusion outcome follows. Partial: welcome Rae but move Kim’s belongings without agreement. Incorrect: extend the visit or require a reason for access preferences. A short visit is not lesser hospitality.
criteria: Visitor and resident needs both shape the plan
Available resources are sufficient without spectacle
Access and timing follow actual agreement

checks.title: Check the changed case
checks.body: No. Respect actual household needs and choose a feasible welcome. Hospitality’s meaning does not require an expense that undermines an existing obligation.
